A black stone like a bean is found in the Nile, and upon seeing it, dogs do not bark. You may also carry a dog's tongue placed under your big toe in your shoe, or carry a dried dog's heart with you, according to Sextus <note>likely Sextus Placitus, author of a 4th-century medicinal text on animal remedies</note>; or carry hare's fur or dung, according to Pliny. Or you may carry the severed tail of a young weasel on your foot, or give the dog a morsel containing a frog; all these things serve to avoid the barking of dogs. Nigidius <note>Publius Nigidius Figulus, a Roman scholar and associate of Cicero</note> says that dogs will flee the sight of a man for an entire day if he removes a tick from a pig and carries it for a little while. Oppianus <note>A Greco-Roman poet known for his works on hunting and fishing</note> says:

> But if you carry a small piece cut from the skin of a hyena,
> Immediately the puppies and fierce dogs will be struck
> With bitter terror, and they shall not bark at you hereafter
> As you walk along, even if they barked before.

### How to make it so a dog cannot run.

If you smear its paws with oil, it will be hindered in its running; it happens in this way.

### How to make a hawk courageous.

You shall encourage the bird against its prey so that it attacks large birds. Moisten the meat which it uses during the hunting season with wine; or if it is a goshawk, give it a little vinegar. When you wish it to fly, give it three morsels of meat moistened with wine, or pour wine from your own mouth into the beak of a pigeon chick, then let the hawk fly. In this way:

### You shall make partridges more combative,

If you give them branches of <term>adiantum</term> <gloss>maidenhair fern</gloss> in their food, according to Pliny; and

### Roosters become more combative,

By giving them garlic in their food just before they are to fight; for which reason they were most wittily called <term>eskorodismenoi</term> <gloss>garlic-fed</gloss> in the Old Comedy <note>a reference to Aristophanes and the practice of feeding garlic to fighting cocks to increase their aggression</note>, a term for one who is vehement and too inclined toward a fight.

### Lest a bird fly into the heights,

Pluck out the tail feathers which direct the course upward; thus it will fly in a circle below. If you wish:

### That a bird be unable to fly,

Cut the upper and lower tendons of the wing, and it remains without further harm; the bird will not fly, and in this way they do not escape from aviaries.

<summary>This page provides various folk remedies and practical techniques for hunters to silence barking dogs, increase the aggression of hawks and fighting roosters using wine and garlic, and prevent birds from escaping aviaries.</summary>
<keywords>animal husbandry, hunting dogs, falconry, cockfighting, Pliny the Elder, Oppian, bird behavior, ancient veterinary medicine</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>shines with piety, religion, prudence, and the worship and veneration of God, as if he had perceived the truth with his own eyes through true reason. By the confidence of his belief, he stands out among men as much as the sun surpasses the other stars with its light. For the sun itself illuminates the other stars not so much by the magnitude of its power as by its divinity and holiness. Believe this sun, O Asclepius, to be the second god, governing all other things and illuminating all worldly creatures, whether they are animate or inanimate.

For if the world is a living being <note>original: "animal mundus"</note> that is always alive, and was, and is, and shall be, then nothing in the world is mortal. Since every single part of a living being is within the world itself—which is like a single, identical, and ever-living animal—there is no place for mortality. Therefore, God himself must be most full of life and eternity, if it is necessary for him to live forever. Thus the sun, just like the world, is sempiternal, and is itself the perpetual governor of living things, or rather the provider and dispenser of their entire vitality. God is therefore the sempiternal governor of the living beings, or the vital things that are in the world, and the eternal dispenser of life itself. He dispensed life once by an eternal law, providing it to all vital things in the manner which I shall now describe.

<summary>Hermes describes the sun as a second god and the eternal governor of life within the world, which is viewed as a single, immortal living being. He explains that because the world is an ever-living entity, nothing within it is truly subject to total mortality.</summary>
<keywords>Asclepius, sun, second god, living world, immortality, eternity, governor of life, divinity, piety</keywords>

Marcus Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a prolific Roman scholar and writer.</note> testifies that he saw these things. And there are things even more wonderful than these: for on the Attic shore, the sea sounds like a lute. At Megara, a certain rock sounds like a lyre when struck with pebbles, so great is the force of Music. It <note>Music</note> soothes the soul, lifts the mind, incites warriors to war, and lessens the labor and fatigue of individual works. It recalls those who have fallen and are in despair, and comforts travelers. And the Arabs say that camels carrying burdens are comforted by their singing drivers. In a similar way, those carrying heavy burdens sing, and are made more capable and relieved by it: for singing produces delight and capability. It mitigates the wrathful, gladdens the sad and anxious, pacifies the discordant, tempers the madness of the frantic, and dissipates vain thoughts. Hence it is that Democritus and Theophrastus affirm that some diseases of the body and mind can be either cured or induced in this way. Thus we read that Terpander and Arion of Methymna <note>Arion was a legendary Greek kitharode; Methymna was a city on Lesbos.</note>...

<summary>This page describes the miraculous physical and psychological effects of music, citing classical authorities and observations of nature and human labor. It highlights music's ability to heal the mind, encourage the weary, and even influence inanimate objects like rocks and water.</summary>
<keywords>Music, Marcus Varro, Megara, Arabs, Democritus, Theophrastus, Terpander, Arion of Methymna, healing, psychology, harmony</keywords>

for the good is innate to truth, along with life and light, and no further avenger has approached. Indeed, all the avengers have been cast out by a sudden impulse. You have understood, my son, the manner of this **rebirth** <note>original: "regenerationis"</note>. When the **number ten** <note>original: "denario numero"; the Decad, representing perfection and the divine powers</note> is present, the intellectual generation is complete, which rejects the **number twelve** <note>original: "duodenarium numerum"; the Duodecad, representing the twelve zodiacal vices</note>. We have observed this from the generation itself. Therefore, whoever loses their bodily senses through the kindness of this divine generation knows themselves to be composed of divine things. Having become steadfast, they rejoice in divine power with their whole mind.

**TATIUS.** O father, I conceive this not by the sight of my eyes, but by the action of the mind, which is exercised through inner powers. I am in heaven, in earth, in water, in air. I am in animals, in trees, in the body, before the body, and after the body. But I wish you would tell me this further: how are the avenging darknesses, twelve in number, repelled by the ten powers? By what means, Trismegistus?

**HERMES.** This tabernacle, O son, is constituted from the **zodiac circle** <note>original: "ex zodiaco circulo"</note>, which consists of that number twelve. The numbers are eleven, but one is all-forming according to the ideas of nature, for the wandering and circuit of man. Thus, those avengers are in a certain way separated from one another, yet in action they are somehow joined together; for example, recklessness is inseparable from wrath. Rightly, therefore, according to correct reason, they are kept at a distance insofar as they are repelled by the ten powers, that is, by the **number ten** <note>original: "denario numero"</note>. For the number ten, O son, is the parent of the soul. Indeed, Life

<summary>Hermes explains how the ten divine powers displace the twelve zodiacal vices during spiritual rebirth, leading Tatius to experience a state of cosmic consciousness. The passage establishes the numerological relationship between the Decad of virtues and the Duodecad of material influences.</summary>
<keywords>rebirth, Decad, Duodecad, zodiac, Tatius, Hermes Trismegistus, cosmic consciousness, numerology, spiritual generation</keywords>

These are followed by the gods whose prince is <term>ousia</term> <gloss>essence or being</gloss>. These are the sensible gods, similar to their dual origin, who produce all things through sensible nature, each one illuminating his own work through the other. Of the heaven, or whatever is comprised by that name, the <term>ousiarches</term> <gloss>ruler of essence</gloss> is Jupiter. For through the heaven, Jupiter provides life to all things. Of the sun, the <term>ousiarches</term> is light. For the good of light is infused into us through the orb of the sun. There are thirty-six <note>referring to the decans of the zodiac</note> whose name is <term>Horoscopoi</term> <gloss>Watchers of the Hour</gloss>, who are always fixed in the same place of the stars. Their <term>ousiarches</term> or prince is he whom they call <term>Pantomorphos</term> <gloss>All-formed or Omniform</gloss>, who creates diverse forms from diverse species. The seven spheres which are called "erratic" <note>the seven wandering planets</note> have their own <term>ousiarchas</term>, that is, their own princes, whom they call Fortune or <term>Heimarmene</term> <gloss>Fate</gloss>, by whom all things are changed by the law of nature with the firmest stability and varied by eternal motion. The air, however, is the instrument or the machine of all things, through which all things are made. Moreover, the <term>ousiarches</term> of this is the second <note>likely referring to the sublunary ruler or a secondary demiurgic force</note>. To mortals belong mortal things, and things similar to them.

Since these things are so, moving from the lowest to the highest, all things pertaining to themselves are naturally connected to one another, so that mortal things are annexed to mortals, and sensible things to sensibles. However, the height of governance obeys that highest Lord, so that they are not many, but rather one. For since all things hang from one, and rather flow down from Him, when they are seen at a distance, they are believed to be many and divided. But united, they are one, or rather two: that from which all things are made, and He by whom they are made. That is, from the matter of which they are made, and by His will, by whose nod other things are effected.

ASCLEPIUS: What is this reasoning again, O Trismegistus?

TRISMEGISTUS: It is such, O Asclepius. For God, or the Father, or the Lord...

<summary>Hermes explains the hierarchy of divine rulers or essences (ousiarchs) governing the heavens, the zodiac, and the planets, concluding that all diverse phenomena flow from a single divine source and will.</summary>
<keywords>Ousia, Ousiarches, Jupiter, Sun, Horoscopoi, Pantomorphos, Seven Spheres, Fate, Heimarmene, Unity of God, Matter</keywords>

brought itself forth. For indeed, arsenic can by no means be fixed <note>rendered non-volatile or solid under heat</note> unless the operator is an artist who equally understands its tinting spirit. In this matter, all the philosophers have truly slumbered, laboring in vain to produce anything from it. Whoever, therefore, is ignorant of this spirit, let him have no hope of fixing the substance itself, nor of attributing to it the power by which he might acquire the perfection of transmutation. For this reason, I make it known to all that the whitening of which mention has been made was drawn from a false foundation; by it, copper is falsely whitened, not changed in its nature. The Sophists <note>deceptive or ignorant practitioners of alchemy</note> mixed <term>Venus</term> <gloss>copper</gloss>—masked and painted in this manner—with twice its weight of <term>Luna</term> <gloss>silver</gloss>, and sold it to goldsmiths and money-changers. Ultimately, they transformed themselves into counterfeiters: not only those who sold it, but also those who bought it. Some of the Sophists took red arsenic in place of the white, and this likewise resulted in a false art. For in whatever way it is prepared, it exhibits nothing but whiteness. Others proceeded further to common sulfur, which they cooked until yellow with vinegar, lye, or very sharp urine, day and night, until a white color emerged. Afterward, they raised it from common salt and the lime of eggshells <note>calcium carbonate from burnt shells</note> through sublimation; they cooked and sublimated it many times. Nevertheless, it always remained combustible, even though it was white. With it, however, they attempted to fix crude mercury

<summary>Paracelsus warns that arsenic cannot be fixed without understanding its "spirit" and exposes how "Sophists" use it to create counterfeit silver. He also describes failed attempts to whiten sulfur using acidic washes and sublimation to stabilize mercury.</summary>

<keywords>arsenic, fixation, transmutation, copper, silver, counterfeiting, sulfur, sublimation, mercury, alchemy</keywords>

they ought to have taken, they instead took <term>pyrite</term>, <term>sulfur</term>, <term>salt</term>, <term>metal</term>, and various other materials in which there is no operation; these are expensive things from the shops, yet in the labor they are of no value at all. Our material, however, is bought from no shop, yet it is found daily in the shop, and merchants cast it out into the streets. It is enough, therefore, that it be found for free. But the material of our <term>stone</term> <gloss>the Philosopher's Stone</gloss> is compared to all those things with which the craftsmen labor. For our stone is <term>our salt</term>, <term>our Mercury</term>, <term>verdigris</term> <gloss>copper rust</gloss>, <term>halonitrum</term> <gloss>saltpeter</gloss>, <term>sal ammoniac</term>, <term>Mars</term> <gloss>iron</gloss>, <term>sulfur</term>, and infinite other things of that kind, yet it is not dug out from wild and rural mountains with hammers and other instruments. Rather, our stone is extracted only from our mountains and springs. In our <term>Salt-spring</term> our <term>Salt</term> is found; from our earth our metal, <term>Mercury</term>, and <term>sulfur</term> are poured, and not from wild, foreign, and rural mountains. The craftsmen do not understand all these things, nor can they believe or comprehend them. For the Lord has darkened and stopped up their senses, for which reason they have used these things otherwise than they ought to have been done, and have missed the mark entirely. Nevertheless, they persisted in that contrary sense and followed their own stubborn heads. For instance, while they ought to have <term>distilled</term> gently, they <term>sublimated</term> <gloss>vaporized to solid</gloss> there with a strong fire, they scorched <term>aqua fortis</term> <gloss>nitric acid</gloss>, and they immediately burned the operation of nature and its substances, reducing them to nothing. Also, when they ought to have <term>dissolved</term>, they <term>coagulated</term> <gloss>solidified</gloss> there, and again, like men unskilled in things, they handled the matter unskillfully. They fell into doubt and repeatedly claimed with lying words that the art was not true but false, in which, however, they themselves are deservedly lying. For their own ignorance has shamefully deceived them, which must be attributed to their own obscure and murky cleverness, while, according to their own dark understanding, they interpreted the words otherwise than they sounded. For example, when the Philosophers spoke of <term>calcining</term> <gloss>reducing to powder by heat</gloss> (which they call grinding), then those unskilled <term>Philosophasters</term> <gloss>pretenders to philosophy</gloss> understood it as burning, and they reduced things entirely to ashes, so that nothing could be made from them. Also, when the Philosophers <term>dissolve</term>, or transmute into water, then those <term>know-it-alls</term> <note>original: "nasutuli", literally "those with big noses" or "the overly inquisitive"</note> burned nature with <term>aqua fortis</term>, and with that same water, which has no...

<summary>The author distinguishes between common chemical substances and the secret materials of the Alchemists, which are found in nature for free. He criticizes "Philosophasters" for misinterpreting metaphorical terms like calcination and dissolution, leading to failed experiments.</summary>
<keywords>Philosopher's Stone, Mercury, Sulfur, Salt, Calcination, Distillation, Aqua Fortis, Philosophasters, Alchemical Materials</keywords>

requires a moderation of the fire, and a gradual succession of its increase, with caution, until it is fixed in its own lime <note>the metallic oxide</note>, lest it easily return into a body <note>revert to a solid metal</note>, so that a greater fire may be administered to it for the perfection of its lime. Similarly, let him not happen to err in <term>Jupiter</term> <gloss>Tin</gloss>, because of its difficult reduction <note>the process of returning a lime to its metallic state</note>; so that if he should ever place its lime into reduction, it might happen that it does not reduce, but he finds it in its prior disposition or reduced into glass, and he deems its reduction impossible. For we say that if one does not apply a great fire in the reduction of <term>Jupiter</term>, it will not reduce. If, however, he applies a great fire, it does not necessarily happen that he reduces it, but it is possible to reduce it into vitrification <note>the process of turning into glass</note>. And this is because <term>Jupiter</term> <margin>am ta</margin> <margin>cc</margin> has a fugitive substance of quicksilver <note>mercury</note> enclosed in the depths of its nature. If this substance endures a long delay in the fire, it will flee, and leave the body deprived of humidity, so that it is found to be converted rather into a state fit for vitrification than for the fusion of a metallic body. For everything deprived of its own humidity gives no fusion except a vitrifying one. Therefore, it is necessarily left that one must hasten to reduce it quickly with a most rapid force of fire. For otherwise it is not reduced. Let him, therefore, be practiced in this, and he shall know. <margin>et</margin> <margin>cc</margin>

The second mode of calcination of these <gloss>Saturn and Jupiter</gloss> two bodies, which is perfected by the sharpness of salt, is that a quantity of salt be thrown upon their surface, quantity after quantity very often during its fusion, and they should be mixed with much agitation by an iron rod <margin>wooden. boiling. see page 57, 14.</margin> over the fire, until through the mixing of salt they are turned into ash. And afterwards, by the same mode of perfection, their lime may be perfected, with its own considerations. But in this there is also a difference in the calcination of these two bodies. Because <term>lead</term> <note>original: plumbum</note> is converted to powder more easily from the first labors of calcination than <term>Jupiter</term> <gloss>Tin</gloss>, yet its lime is not perfected more easily than that of <term>Jupiter</term>. The cause of this depends on the fact that <term>Saturn</term> <gloss>Lead</gloss> has a more fixed humidity than <term>Jupiter</term>.

829. Since Religion resides in the highest parts of a man, and from those highest parts his lower parts live and shine, and because Mohammed is present in their minds along with their Religion, someone representing Mohammed is always placed in their sight. So that they may turn their faces toward the East, over which the Lord is, he is placed below the Christian <term>Meditullium</term> <gloss>center point</gloss>. This is not the actual Mohammed who wrote the Koran, but another who performs his office; nor is it always the same person, for he is changed. Once it was a man from Saxony who, having been captured by Algerians and becoming a Mohammedan, and because he had also been a Christian, was sometimes moved to speak with them about the Lord—that He was not the son of Joseph, but the Son of God Himself. Other men succeeded this Mohammed later. In the place where that representative Mohammed has his seat, a fire appears like torches so that he may be known; but that fire is not visible to any others except the Mohammedans.

830. The actual Mohammed who wrote the Koran does not come into view today. I was told that in the earliest times he presided over them, but because he wished to rule over all things of their Religion as a God, he was ejected from his seat (which he held beneath the Roman Catholics) and sent down to the right side near the south. Once, a certain society of Mohammedans was incited by malicious spirits to acknowledge Mohammed as God; to settle the sedition, Mohammed was raised up from the lower earth and shown, and then he was also seen by me. He appeared similar to corporeal spirits who have no interior perception, with a face verging toward black, and I heard him speaking these words: *I am your Mohammed*; and soon he seemed to sink back down.

831. The Mohammedans are hostile to Christians primarily because of the faith in three Divine Persons, and the resulting worship of three Gods, as many Creators; and toward the Roman Catholics additionally because of their kneeling before images. For this reason they call the latter Idolaters and the former fanatics, saying that they make a three-headed God, and that they say "one" but mutter "three," consequently splitting Omnipotence and making three out of the one and only. They say Christians are like <term>Fauns</term> <gloss>mythological goat-men</gloss> with three horns, one for each God, and yet three for one; and that they thus pray, thus sing, and thus sound from their pulpits.

832. The Mohammedans, like all nations who acknowledge one God and love what is just and do good from a religious motive, have their own Heaven, but outside the Christian one. Yet the Mohammedan Heaven is divided into two: in the lower one they live honestly with several wives, but from there none are elevated into the higher Heaven except those who give up their concubines and acknowledge the Lord our Savior, and at the same time His dominion over Heaven and Hell. I heard that it is impossible for them to think that God the Father and our Lord are one, but that it is possible for them to believe that He rules over the Heavens and Hells because He is the Son of God the Father. This is the Faith among them through which an ascent into the higher Heaven is granted to them by the Lord.

833. That the Mohammedan Religion has been received by more kingdoms than the Christian Religion can be a scandal <note>a cause of doubt or stumbling</note> to those who think about Divine Providence and at the same time believe that no one can be saved except those born Christian. But the Mohammedan Religion is not a scandal to those who believe that all things are of Divine Providence; these people search for the reason why it is so, and they find it. It is in this: that the Mohammedan Religion acknowledges the Lord as the Greatest Prophet, the Wisest of all, and also as the Son of God; but because they have made the Koran alone the Book of their religion, and thus Mohammed (who wrote it) has settled in their thoughts and they follow him with some worship, they think little about our Lord. So that it may be fully known that this Religion was raised up by the Divine Providence of the Lord to destroy the idolatries of many nations, it will be described in some order; but first, concerning the origin of idolatries. Before that Religion, there was idolatrous worship

<summary>Swedenborg describes the state of Muslims in the spiritual world, their rejection of the Trinity and images, and their specific Heavens. He explains that Islam was established by Divine Providence to eliminate widespread idolatry among various nations.</summary>
<keywords>Mohammedans, Islam, Koran, Trinity, Idolatry, Divine Providence, Spiritual World, Representative Mohammed, Monotheism</keywords>

plainly, the greatest part of diseases coming from celestial Influence and from the Astral Impression of the Firmament of the Greater World <note>the Macrocosm or universe</note> does not wish to be cured by indiscriminate remedies, such as through the <term>Arcana</term> <gloss>secret essences</gloss> of herbs, minerals, or metals. Instead, the cure should be established through Astronomical Influence, at least with those things which have an analogy to the greater and lesser world <note>the Microcosm or man</note>. In these things resides the true Magnetic power of the Firmament and the Celestial Impression for resisting diseases from the Firmament of the greater and lesser world, as appears in Water-pepper, Goldenrod, Tarragon, and Comfrey.

If a disease or pain is inflicted Supernaturally through incantation or a Magical Impression of the Ascendants, then the healing efforts of the first three <note>referring to the first three Beings or categories of disease</note> are useless. According to Paracelsus, one must proceed Magically and Supernaturally, and the evil must be repelled in the same manner in which it was inflicted. Otherwise, in the said Simples <note>medicinal herbs</note> there is an Influential attraction, and they cure all things by Divine ordination Magically, Astronomically, and Magnetically, because the medicine is in them and the Magnet is in Man. For just as the Sun and Stars have the power of attracting moisture from lower things, so Man (by his innate magnetic attractive power, like a Magnet drawing the spirit of iron in place of nourishment) and lower things have the same power of attracting from Higher things, as we see in the time of Plague; and these chemical...

CLXXXVI.
### ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,

### On the images of the head and tail of the dragon of the Moon. Cap. XLV.

<note>A woodcut illustration depicting a serpent or dragon coiled into a circular shape resembling the Greek letter Theta (Θ). The creature has the head of a hawk and a pointed tail. Within the circular body, there is a central vertical line crossed by a shorter horizontal line, with small astrological or symbolic marks at the terminals.</note>

They also made an image of the head and tail of the dragon of the Moon <note>the lunar nodes, where the Moon's path crosses the ecliptic</note>, namely the likeness of a serpent between the aerial and fiery circle, with the head of a hawk surrounding them, in the likeness of the Greek letter <term>theta</term> <gloss>Θ</gloss>. They made it when Jupiter with the Head <note>the North Node</note> held the midheaven. They affirm that this image contributes much to the success of petitions. They intended to signify a good and happy <term>daemon</term> <gloss>spirit or guiding intelligence</gloss> through this image, and they wished to represent him by the image of a serpent. By "atmosphere," he means the **void** <note>original: *al-khalā’*, the vacuum or empty space</note>, since the world could have occupied a different position within that void. From this, he concluded that the world was created through **Will** <note>original: *irāda*</note>. 

The premise stating that the Will is what specifies one of two identical possibilities is correct. However, the premise stating that the world exists within a surrounding void is false, or at least not self-evident. Furthermore, his assumption of this void leads to a conclusion they find repulsive: that the void would have to be eternal. This is because if the void were created in time, it would itself require another void to exist within.

As for the premise stating that Will can only produce a created <note>original: *muḥdath*, something that begins to exist in time</note> object of will, that is not self-evident. This is because the **Will in act** <note>original: *al-irāda bi-l-fi‘l*, the actualized exercise of will</note> exists simultaneously with the action upon the object of will itself. Will belongs to the category of **relational terms** <note>original: *al-muḍāf*</note>. It has been demonstrated that when one of two relational terms exists in act, the other must also exist in act, such as father and son; and if one exists in potentiality, the other exists in potentiality. Therefore, if the Will in act is created in time, the object of will must necessarily be created in time. But if the Will in act is eternal, then the object of will in act is eternal.

As for the will that precedes the object of will, that is the **Will in potentiality** <note>original: *al-irāda bi-l-quwwa*</note>. I mean the will whose object has not yet emerged into actuality, because the action necessitating the creation of the object has not yet been joined to that will. For this reason, it is clear that when its object does emerge, the Will enters a state of existence it was not in before the object emerged into actuality, since the Will was the cause of the object’s creation through the mediation of the act. Thus, if the **Theologians** <note>original: *al-Mutakallimūn*, scholars of Kalam who used rational arguments to defend Islamic creed</note> were to posit that the Will is created in time, it would necessarily follow that the object of will is created in time.

The apparent meaning of the **Divine Law** <note>original: *al-Shar‘*</note> is that it did not delve into such depths with the common people. Therefore, it did not explicitly state whether the Will is eternal or created in time. Rather, it stated what most clearly suggests that the Will brings created beings into existence, as in the words of the Exalted: "Our word to a thing, when We will it, is only that We say to it: 'Be,' and it is" <note>Quran 16:40</note>. This was done because the common people do not understand how created beings can arise from an eternal Will. But the unlearned and those of a nature for whom a true fate from the Lord did not proceed to obtain gifts, nor to have knowledge of immortal Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus, here used by Porphyry to refer to the supreme deity.</note>, not listening to both gods and divine men, have indeed rejected all gods; but they have chosen not only to follow the prohibited demons with no hatred, but even to revere them. While pretending to worship God, they do not perform those things alone through which God is adored. For God indeed, as the father of all, needs nothing; but it is well for us when we adore him through justice and chastity and other virtues, making our very life a prayer to him through imitation and instruction concerning him. For instruction purifies, he says, and imitation deifies the affection by working toward him. He indeed preached well concerning God the Father and said by what customs he is to be worshipped. The prophetic books of the Hebrews are full of these precepts, when the life of the saints is either praised or blamed. But among Christians, there was only so much, or he only slanders as much as the demons whom he thinks are gods wish; as if it were difficult for anyone to recall what shameful and disgraceful things were performed in theaters and temples in service to the gods, and to attend to what is read, said, and heard in churches, or what is offered to the true God; and from this to understand where the building and where the ruin of morals lies. But who said this to him or inspired it, except a diabolical spirit—so vain and apt a lie—that the Christians revere rather than hate the demons prohibited from being worshipped by the Hebrews? But that God whom the wise men of the Hebrews worshipped, and the celestial holy angels and powers of God—whom we venerate and love as most blessed citizens in this our mortal pilgrimage—forbids sacrifice, thundering in his law which he gave to his Hebrew people; and he brought it in very threateningly, saying: He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out. And lest anyone should think it was commanded that sacrifice not be made to the most wicked demons and earthly spirits, whom this man calls the least or lesser ones—since in the holy scriptures they themselves are called gods, not of the Hebrews

<column-break/>

but of the nations: which the seventy interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> evidently placed in the psalm, saying: For all the gods of the nations are demons. Lest anyone therefore should think it was prohibited to these demons indeed, but permitted to sacrifice to all or some of the celestial beings, he immediately added: except to the Lord alone; that is, except to the Lord only. Lest perhaps he who says "to the Lord alone" should believe that there is only one God to whom he thinks sacrifice should be made. That this is not to be understood so is very easily found in the Greek scriptures. Therefore the God of the Hebrews, to whom even this great philosopher <note>Porphyry.</note> offers such great testimony, gave a law to his Hebrew people, written in the Hebrew language; not obscure and unknown, but now spread abroad among all nations, in which law it is written: He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, except to the Lord only. What need is there to search for many things in this his law and his prophets concerning this matter? Rather, not to search: for they are not hidden or erased, but plain and frequent to collect and to place in this my disputation, by which it appears clearer than light that he willed sacrifice to be made to no one at all except to himself, the true and supreme God. Behold this one thing, briefly yet grandly, threateningly, but truly said by that God whom the most learned of them preach as so excellent: let them hear, let them fear, let them fulfill it, lest eradication follow the disobedient. He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, he says, except to the Lord only. Not because he has need of anything, but because it is profitable for us that we should be his property. For to him it is sung in the holy writings of the Hebrews: I have said to the Lord, you are my God, since you do not need my goods. Moreover, we ourselves are his most noble and best sacrifice. This is his city, the mystery of which we celebrate with our offerings, which are known to the faithful, just as we have discussed in the preceding books. For the Hebrew prophets foretold through oracles that the victims which the Jews offered in the shadow of the future would cease, and that the nations from the rising of the sun to its setting would offer one sacrifice, just as we now see being done.

## Main Text (Zohar)

**Rabbi Eleazar** spoke to Isaac: Who is the "crushed one" <note>original: *dekya katya*</note>? Isaac bowed his head. Isaac was thin and "crushed," and he was concerned for his portion <note>the attribute of Judgment</note>. Heaven forbid that he was angry, but his portion was not like the others. For behold, Isaac is from the side of **Lovingkindness** <note>term: Chesed</note> that is bowed down. And it is asked: Are not all of them **Judgment** <note>term: Din</note>? They are from the side of **Mercy** <note>term: Rachamim</note> that is bowed, and Mercy is the King. Wisdom inherits Lovingkindness, for Lovingkindness bows, and Isaac as Judgment is from Lovingkindness. Isaac bows in Mercy, from the side of harsh Judgment. And so it was above, this one from that one, and this one emerged from that one, until everything was known as one. And they all hang from one another, and for everything to be found as one, the Heavens are needed forever and ever.

**Rabbi Eleazar** recognized that there are no paths for it when we see it as one, and one is desired in both of them to complete the whole, such as Jacob. And this is what is written:
> And the middle bolt in the midst of the boards shall pass through **from end to end.** <note>Exodus 26:28</note>

This proves everything; for if you do not read it except from our side and from our side, everything is known as being able to rise in one **balance** <note>term: matkala</note>. It does not change and shall not be changed, as it is written:
> **I am the Lord, I change not.** <note>Malachi 3:6</note>

**Rabbi Judah** said: All of them are shining cups, hanging from one another, and their foundation is one whole, not to be separated. And whoever separates them by his own power is separated from the Life of Worlds. **Rabbi Isaac** said: It is written:
> **And I will give children to be their princes, and babes shall rule over them.** <note>Isaiah 3:4</note>

This is what is written regarding the "bold-faced" **Cherubim** <note>term: Keruvim</note>. And it is written, "He who sits upon the Cherubim," and it is written, "And He rode upon a Cherub and did fly." "He who sits upon the Cherubim" refers to when He dwells to be settled in assistance; it is written "He who sits upon the Cherubim" when He is found in perfection. "And He rode upon a Cherub" <note>singular</note> refers to when the King is not settled upon His throne. "He who sits upon the Cherubim" <note>plural</note> refers to two. Woe to the world when one Cherub turns his face away from his fellow, for behold it is written:
> **And their faces shall look one to another.** <note>Exodus 26:20</note>

This is when there was peace in the world. **Rabbi Isaac** said: We have learned, "The nakedness of your daughter-in-law and the daughters of your father-in-law you shall not uncover." Woe to him who uncovers their nakedness. In this manner, it is written of Jacob that he "passed through from end to end." And so the portion of Israel for the Holy One, blessed be He, is found in their adornments, in the likeness of that which is above, as it is written:
> **Israel, in whom I will be glorified.** <note>Isaiah 49:3</note>

Come and see, **Rabbi Isaac** said: In former days, when one said to his fellow, "Show me one vessel and take money for it." Now a man says to his fellow, "Take money and show me another," and there is no one to taste and no one to incline his portion, except for those few who are gathered and supreme before the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is written:
> **Thy people also shall be all righteous: they shall inherit the land for ever, the branch of my planting, the work of my hands, that I may be glorified.** <note>Isaiah 60:21</note>

Woe that the money is filled and sustained. **Rabbi Isaac** said: Woe, for I see those who are circumcised, all those who are crowned and stand in the upper heights. Woe that it is filled, and all those below hang in sorrow, woe. A window was opened for us, opened and polished and prepared from the smoke to the order that is upon them. And as in the Book of Concealment <note>term: Sifra de-Tzniuta</note> it is proven: woe above, woe below, and all of them rise in one balance. What is the "Concealment of the Book"? **Rabbi Hezekiah said:** These are the chapters that are all in the Great Palace and fill all the earth. **Rabbi Judah** said: All of them are superior in this way. **The Rabbi said:** Woe to him who bends and bows, and to him who does not rise and bow to them in this way.

### The Parable of the Wheat

A parable of a man who lived among the fields and did not know the dwellers of the city. He sowed wheat and ate the wheat in its raw form. One day he entered the city, and they brought him a good loaf of bread. He said, "What is this man-made thing for?" They said, "It is bread to eat." He ate it and found it very pleasant to his taste. **The Rabbi said:** "From what is this made?" They said, "Wheat." Later they brought him cakes kneaded in oil. He tasted them and said, "And what are these made of?" They said, "Wheat." Later they brought him royal pastries made with honey and oil. He said, "And what are these sweets made of?" They said, "Wheat." He said, "Surely I am the master of all these things, for I eat the essence of all these, which is wheat." And because of that...

->1<-
The heave-offering <term>terumah</term> <gloss>the portion of the harvest given to the priest</gloss> and the first fruits <term>bikkurim</term>
are alike in that one is liable for the penalty of death <note>by the hands of Heaven, for intentional consumption by a non-priest</note> and the payment of an added fifth <note>of the value, if consumed unintentionally</note> on their account.
They are forbidden to non-priests <term>zarim</term> <gloss>literally "strangers," meaning anyone not of the priestly line</gloss>.
They are the property of the priest.
They are neutralized <note>if accidentally mixed with common produce</note> in a ratio of one to one hundred and one.
They require the washing of hands <note>before handling</note> and the setting of the sun <note>for a priest who was impure to become pure enough to eat them</note>.
Behold, these rules apply to <term>terumah</term> and <term>bikkurim</term>,
which is not the case for the tithe <term>ma'aser</term> <gloss>specifically the Second Tithe, which was eaten by the owner in Jerusalem</gloss>.

There are rules that apply to the tithe and the first fruits which do not apply to <term>terumah</term>:
For the tithe and the first fruits require being brought to a specific place <note>Jerusalem</note>,

And it is forbidden to eat any amount of them outside of Jerusalem,
and their offspring <note>the produce grown from their seeds</note> is forbidden to be eaten in Jerusalem,
even to non-priests and to livestock.
Rabbi Shimon permits.
Behold, these rules apply to the tithe and the first fruits,
which is not the case for <term>terumah</term>.

### Chapter on their various sects, their doctrines, their signs, their stations, and their stories.

I have mentioned previously in the account of Abu al-Hasan al-Nuri <note>a famous Sufi of Baghdad, d. 907 CE</note> that they consist of twelve groups. Two of them are rejected, and ten are accepted. Each class among them possesses a beautiful way of dealing with God <note>original: "muʿāmalat"</note> and a praised path in spiritual struggles <note>term: mujāhadāt <gloss>strenuous self-discipline</gloss></note> and a refined etiquette in contemplations <note>term: mushāhadāt <gloss>witnessing the Divine</gloss></note>. Although they differ in their dealings, struggles, contemplations, and ascetic practices, they are in agreement and accord regarding the principles and branches of the Religious Law and the Unity of God <note>term: tawḥīd <gloss>the oneness of God</gloss></note>. Abu Yazid <note>the famous mystic Bayazid al-Bistami</note> said: The disagreement of the scholars is a mercy, except regarding the simplification of the Unity of God. This is in accord with a well-known tradition.

<margin>

</margin>

The reality of <term>tasawwuf</term> <gloss>Sufism</gloss> lies between the reports of the masters from the perspective of Truth <note>original: "ḥaqīqat"</note> and what is distributed from the perspective of metaphor and external forms. Therefore, by way of brevity and conciseness, I shall speak on the explanation of that distribution

and I shall spread out a carpet regarding the fundamental doctrine of each one, so that the seeker may gain knowledge of it, the scholars may have a weapon, the disciples may find rectitude, and the lovers may find success.

The term "perfect" <note>Hebrew: *Tamim*</note> contains the secret of two things. Therefore it says "His work is perfect," for He consulted both Judgment and Mercy before decreeing the sentence. This is the secret of "True Judgment."

Regarding the phrase "For all His ways are justice" <note>Deuteronomy 32:4</note>, this means it is visible to every eye, as it says "For all His ways are justice." ### **Torah** Or <gloss>Torah Light</gloss>
These commandments mentioned in this portion are divided into three parts, which are the three pillars upon which the world stands: Torah, Divine Service <term>Avodah</term>, and Acts of Loving-kindness <term>Gemilut Hasadim</term>.

**Torah** consists of the prohibitions "Do not add" and "Do not subtract," which indicate the perfection of the Torah. This is as the philosophers have said: a thing that is perfectly complete cannot be said to be lacking or excessive. For if it were lacking, it would not be complete; and if it could receive an addition, it follows that it was not previously complete. Therefore, the definition of "complete" is that which has neither deficiency nor excess. It is known that the Torah is dependent on His Great Name, which is <term>Y-H-V-H</term>, as in "The Torah of the Lord <note>Y-H-V-H</note> is perfect" <note>Psalm 19:8</note>, as I have elaborated in my commentary on Tractate Shevuot in the chapter "Torah Or." And as it says in the Zohar on the verse "This is My name and this is My memorial" <note>Exodus 3:15</note>: the letters <term>Y-H</term> with "My name" <term>Shemi</term> equals 365 <note>the number of negative commandments</note>; the letters <term>V-H</term> with "My memorial" <term>Zichri</term> equals 248 <note>the number of positive commandments</note>. It is written, "I am the first and I am the last" <note>Isaiah 44:6</note>; He is the absolute perfection, without deficiency or addition. Regarding this comes the warning: "You shall not do so to the Lord your God" <note>Deuteronomy 12:4</note>—a warning against erasing the Name or breaking a stone from the Holy Temple. Behold, the letters of the Name are the "house" in which He, may He be blessed, dwells, as is the Temple. It is written, "I am the Lord, that is My name" <note>Isaiah 42:8</note>; the letters are like a frame for the house, and His Name, may He be blessed, is the soul within them. One who destroys His house, as it were, destroys Him. This is the secret of "You shall not do so to the Lord your God."

**Divine Service** <term>Avodah</term> comprises most of the commandments mentioned in this portion. The command came to have a fixed place in the Chosen House, and the text gives the reason: "To His habitation shall you seek, and there you shall come" <note>Deuteronomy 12:5</note>. "To His habitation" <term>Le-shichno</term> hints at the Divine Presence <term>Shekhinah</term>, which is the Palace of the Name <term>Y-H-V-H</term>. Do not fear that she <note>the Shekhinah</note> will dwell there, for in the Temple, the Glory <term>Kavod</term> is unified with the Beauty <term>Tiferet</term> of His people. This is "to place His name there," which the Targum <note>Aramaic translation</note> renders as "to cause His Presence to dwell." And "round about the holy place the wicked walk" <note>Psalm 12:9</note>, referring to the shells of impurity <term>Kelipot</term>; therefore, "Take heed to yourself that you do not offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see" <note>Deuteronomy 12:13</note>.

### **Sometimes**
Sparks of holiness spread outward, and it is a commandment to return them and bring them inside. This is the secret of the commandment to bring the firstborn sacrifices from outside the city to the Chosen House. Then the branch returns to its root, and it is written of them, "There you shall offer" <note>Deuteronomy 12:14</note>—meaning there they shall have an ascent <term>Aliyah</term>, and not outside. Since the holiness resides in the Chosen House, which is in the Holy Land, we are commanded to "turn away from evil" by destroying all the places where the nations worshipped. One must uproot and eradicate them, and this was commanded specifically in the Holy Land. The secret of this hints that the ten nations <note>of Canaan</note> were not merely idolaters; rather, the nations in the Land of Israel, being under the direct governance of the Honorable Name, worship the Lord through "cutting the saplings" <note>a metaphor for heresy/dualism</note>, which is actual idolatry. However, outside the Land, they are under the governance of external forces. Just as there is a great prohibition against breaking a single stone of holiness, so conversely, it is a great commandment to destroy and eliminate a "Subverted City" <term>Ir HaNidachat</term> and never to rebuild it, for its place is impure. Likewise, one must uproot the "Enticer" <term>Mesit</term> and "Seducer" <term>Madiach</term>, for he stems from the impurity of the Ancient Serpent who was an enticer. The Holy One, blessed be He, immediately said, "Cursed is the serpent"; therefore, the powers of the <term>Samael</term> <note>the angel of evil</note> are never to be appeased. The command came not to love him and not to listen to him, as was said of the serpent: "And I will put enmity between you and the woman" <note>Genesis 3:15</note>. A false prophet is also like an enticer.

Let us return to the matter: the root of holiness is the Chosen House and Jerusalem. This is the reason for the First Fruits <term>Bikkurim</term>, which the priests have no permission to eat until they are placed in the Chosen House. For the first fruits, being the "beginning," indicate great holiness; therefore, they must go to the holy place, and from there they take their wisdom, for they are holy to God, and they shall eat in Jerusalem. The secret of "Lesser Holy" sacrifices and the Second Tithe is that they are eaten in Jerusalem. This is the "grain, wine, and oil," which are the "fathers of fathers" of all sustenance. It is forbidden to eat Lesser Holy sacrifices until after the sprinkling of their blood, for the blood is the soul <term>Nefesh</term>, and only afterward is there permission to enjoy the meat. Know that just as the Service <term>Avodah</term>—the sacrifice—is an offering to the Lord, so too is the worshiper. For the essence of the service is that one sacrifices himself, in the secret of "When a man <term>Adam</term> brings an offering from among you" <note>Leviticus 1:2</note>. The burnt offering <term>Olah</term> is entirely consumed, for it comes to atone for the thoughts of the heart <note>spiritual transgressions</note>, and it is burned all night so the Serpent cannot hinder it. Lesser Holy sacrifices represent the peace of the soul and the body.

### **The Secret**
Of the firstborn is the secret of "Holy Israel," who are called "Israel My firstborn" <note>Exodus 4:22</note>. He has compassion on them and guards them, and they are called "the sheep of My pasture." Therefore, the firstborn animal is eaten only by the priests. The secret of eating sacrifices corresponds to those with blemishes... for Holy Israel are called "Man" <term>Adam</term>. He was originally holy, but afterward a blemish fell upon him after he sinned and was clothed in "garments of skin," yet he has a redemption through the secret of "I will give a man <term>Adam</term> in your stead" <note>Isaiah 43:4</note>. This was the secret of the Scapegoat <term>Azazel</term> which "bears their iniquities" <note>Leviticus 16:22</note>—meaning the iniquities that rest upon his head and his people. But we are commanded not to cause a blemish in a consecrated animal in order to eat it. For if one intentionally blemishes the holy, he damages the root. There is also a prohibition against working or shearing consecrated animals, for even the "broken tablets" <note>of the Ten Commandments</note> remain holy.

### **The General Principle**
The Service is the sacrifice, but the internal sacrifice is the Man himself. Likewise, his soul is called to the "Altar Above" after death, where Michael is the High Priest. This is the secret: "In the image of God He made man." Therefore, the warning came to be careful during his life regarding damages to souls—not to kill a person except after thorough inquiry and investigation. Then, he is "dead by the hand of Heaven," in the secret of "He is the witness, He is the judge," for the Lord is the True Witness and True Judge. So must the Sanhedrin be: just as they are judges of truth, they must have witnesses of truth. I mean they must clarify the truth of the witnesses with complete clarity—inquiry and investigation—and then their judgment is like the judgment of Heaven. "Precious in the eyes of the Lord is the death of His pious ones" <note>Psalm 116:15</note>.

### **And Since**
Death is precious in the eyes of the Lord—because Israel are holy from the side of their souls, which after death cleave to the heights—therefore the command came: "You shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness..." <note>Deuteronomy 14:1</note>, for "You are children to the Lord your God." This is not the case for the nations; cutting and baldness are their customs, as is fitting for them, since at death they go to perdition and have no portion in this world or the World to Come. We, however, are children of the Lord. When we depart from this world, which is a temporary dwelling, we instead have a permanent residence above with our Father in Heaven. Therefore, it is forbidden to mourn excessively or perform these acts.

### **Let us return**
To the matter: the person who worships is himself the sacrifice, as it says, "When a man brings an offering from among you." There is a further secret here: for the spark that fell even to the lower levels of man—that is, in the secret of reincarnation <term>Gilgul</term>—"Man and beast You save, O Lord" <note>Psalm 36:7</note>. Therefore, even in eating non-consecrated meat <term>Chullin</term>, we were commanded regarding ritual slaughter <term>Shechitah</term> with great care, without any nick in the blade. For if there is a nick, it becomes a carcass <term>Nevelah</term>, and "a disgrace <term>Nevelah</term> is committed in Israel." For who knows what reincarnation is within it? "Love your neighbor as yourself"—choose for him a "beautiful death," namely, slaughter without a nick. If the animal dies on its own, the power of impurity takes hold of it. But when one slaughters it properly, and there is in the animal or pure bird a spark of holiness, then its soul departs in purity.

### **One who eats**
A limb from a living animal <term>Ever Min HaChai</term> is like eating the flesh of a brother when a reincarnated soul is present. This is the secret of "You shall not eat the soul with the flesh" <note>Deuteronomy 12:23</note>. Likewise, the prohibition of forbidden foods and the signs of pure animals, beasts, and birds all indicate the spark spread within them—whether it is from the "Side of Impurity" <term>Sitra Achra</term> or the "Side of Holiness" <term>Sitra de-Kedusha</term>. I elaborated on this in Parashat Shemini. When Israel conducts itself with holiness, it is written of them: "And they shall make for Me a sanctuary, and I will dwell within them" <note>Exodus 25:8</note>. For they themselves are the Tabernacle, as man is divided into three parts: the head corresponds to the Holy of Holies; the heart to the Holy Place; and from the belly downward to the Courtyard, as I elaborated in Parashat Terumah. When one eats foods from the side of holiness, they are like sacrifices offered upon the Altar. Regarding this, our Sages said: "Now, a man's table atones for him," as I have explained elsewhere.

### **The matter**
Of the commandments of the Festivals and their sacrifices, I have written about each in its specific place. The command came to rejoice on the festivals and to go up on the pilgrimage: "Three times a year all your males shall appear." Do not read it only as "appearing" <note>to see</note> but also "to be seen." Therefore, if one wishes to be seen in the Holy Temple where the Glory dwells, he must "turn from evil and do good" and be a faithful servant to his Creator. Otherwise, it is forbidden for a wicked person to enter the hall; how could he wish to be seen before Him, may He be blessed, and bring a burnt offering of appearance? For then he himself is the sacrifice through the sacrifice he offers. It says "Three times a year he shall appear"—referring to Isaac, who was a "perfect burnt offering."

Other things are with it, and the one who has undergone <term>evacuation</term> <gloss>istifragh; the removal of excess humors</gloss> must not rush to consume many or heavy foods, for <term>nature</term> <gloss>the body's innate healing power</gloss> will attract them while they are undigested. If any of that is necessary, it must be taken little by little, spaced out so that it is gradual, ensuring that what enters the body is well-digested. <term>Venesection</term> <gloss>al-fasd; bloodletting</gloss> is the evacuation specific to the <term>equable</term> <gloss>as-sawiyyah; balanced humors</gloss>. As for the evacuation specific to a humor that is excessive in quantity alone or corrupt in quality, it is not venesection. Every excessive evacuation usually causes vomiting. 

If the cessation of a habitual diarrhea causes a disease, the cause for the return of that disease is usually the accumulation of that evacuation. For example, if the cessation of a nosebleed or mucus discharge causes blockages, then their return will remove them. Know that the remaining matter that needs evacuation is less receptive to complete extraction; if one persists until it is fully exhausted, the patient's strength will fail. Often, nature dissolves that remainder on its own. As long as the humor is of the type that should be expelled and the patient can bear it, do not fear excess; sometimes you may need to evacuate until <term>fainting</term> <gloss>al-ghashi</gloss> occurs. 

For one whose strength is robust but whose bad humors are plentiful, evacuate them little by little. Likewise, if the matter is highly <term>mature</term> <gloss>nadhj; ripened for expulsion</gloss> or heavily mixed with the blood, it cannot be evacuated all at once. This occurs in cases of sciatica, chronic joint pain, cancer, chronic scabies, and chronic boils. Know that purging draws from above and uproots from below, so it is consistent with the accustomed attraction <note>of the body's waste</note>. It is also suitable after the materials have settled. If the materials are below, drawing them to the opposite direction <note>upward</note> and uprooting them from where they are is done by attraction and vice versa. The state of venesection differs according to the sites from which the blood is taken, as you have learned. Those who least need evacuation are those with good digestion, and inhabitants of hot countries have little need for evacuation.

We say: it is recommended for one who wishes to take a purgative to restrict or divide their food firmly. First, the amount they should try in a day should be in stages, using different foods and different drinks. In this state, the stomach will desire to push what is in it upward or downward. As for non-varied food, the stomach becomes saturated with it, grows heavy, and grips it tightly, especially if the amount is small. For those with naturally loose bowels, none of this is necessary. Know that the need for vomiting, purging, and the like does not occur in those who follow a <term>good regimen</term> <gloss>husn al-tadbir</gloss>; they require something lighter. Often, exercise, massage, and cupping are sufficient for them. 

If the body becomes overfilled with the best of humors—meaning blood—then venesection is what is needed for cleansing, rather than purging. If necessity dictates venesection or evacuation in the autumn, begin with vomiting and delay venesection; this is among the counsels of Hippocrates and the writings of <term>Abila</term> <gloss>likely a reference to a commentator or physician</gloss>, and it is the truth. Likewise, if phlegmatic humors are mixed with the blood. However, if the humors are equal, viscous, and cold, venesection may increase their thickness and viscosity; in that case, one must begin with purging. In general, if the humors are equal, prioritize venesection, and if an evacuation is still needed after that, proceed. If they are unequal, evacuate the excess first until they are equal, then perform venesection. 

Whoever prioritizes medicine over venesection should have performed venesection a few days prior. If someone has recently undergone venesection and needs evacuation, drinking medicine will be more effective for them. Often, drinking medicine when venesection was actually required results in vomiting and distress; if it does not settle with sedatives, then venesection should have preceded it. There is no evacuation required for excessive fullness that the severity of the illness and the fullness in quality and quantity do not call for. Often, a good regimen makes the required venesection unnecessary at the time. Often, a call for evacuation arises but is countered by an obstacle; in that case, the only trick is fasting, sleep, and correcting the <term>dyscrasia</term> <gloss>su' mizaj; imbalance of temperament</gloss> caused by the fullness. 

Some evacuations are for the sake of <term>precaution</term> <gloss>istizhar</gloss>, such as what is needed by those accustomed to gout, epilepsy, or other conditions at a known time, especially in the spring. One needs to take precautions before the time and perform the specific evacuation, whether it be venesection or purging. Sometimes the use of external drying agents and desiccating medicines acts as an evacuation, as is done for those with dropsy. You may need to use a medicine that matches the humor being evacuated in quality, such as <term>scammony</term> <gloss>saqmunia</gloss> when you need to evacuate yellow bile; in that case, you must mix it with something that opposes it in quality but agrees with it in purging, such as <term>myrobalan</term> <gloss>halilaj</gloss>. 

If a dyscrasia occurs afterward in those with inflammation of the viscera, their purging becomes weak. If forced to do so, use for them things like <term>bindweed</term> <gloss>lablab</gloss> and <term>safflower</term> <gloss>qartham</gloss>. As for the purgative and <term>cassia fistula</term> <gloss>khiyar shanbar</gloss>, Hippocrates said: "He whose constitution is easy, responding naturally to vomiting, the first step in his cleansing is to use vomiting in the summer or spring." This protects the body from exhaustion. Know that one who is accustomed to loose bowels or is not used to vomiting in the summer should avoid it unless necessary. One must <term>bind</term> <gloss>ya'qid; stabilize</gloss> before purging and vomiting by thinning the humor intended for evacuation and widening the channels. 

Know that for one who has loose bowels or is unaccustomed to vomiting, using strong medicine without prior preparation—such as reducing food—makes purging and vomiting difficult, exhausting, and causes a mixing of humors. An emetic medicine may turn into a purgative if the stomach is strong, if taken during extreme hunger, if the drinker has loose bowels, or if the medicine is of a heavy substance that descends quickly. Conversely, a purgative may become an emetic due to weakness of the stomach, extreme heaviness, the medicine being repulsive, or the person having indigestion. 

Every purgative medicine, if it does not purge due to lack of <term>maturation</term> <gloss>nadhj</gloss>, will stir the humor it is meant to purge and spread it through the body, overcoming the body and drawing other humors to it, thus increasing that humor in the body. Some humors respond more quickly to vomiting, such as yellow bile; others are resistant to vomiting, such as black bile. Some have a specific state, like phlegm, where purging is more correct for it. For those whose humor is descending, such as those with <term>slippery intestines</term> <gloss>zalaq al-am'a; chronic diarrhea</gloss>, the intestines grip, making purgative medicines difficult. Medicines composed of highly different ingredients in their purging time cause distress; the first may purge the second before the second can act, or the first may purge the second itself. 

Whoever undergoes purging while their body is clean will inevitably suffer from medicine-induced pain, colic, and distress, and the evacuation will be very difficult. In general, when medicine evacuates waste, there is no distress; if it is taken with distress, it is either evacuating something other than waste, or the humor being evacuated has changed. If the humor evacuated by vomiting or purging changes to another humor, it indicates the body has been cleansed of the intended humor.

### Question 85, Article 3

The third article: whether more universal things are prior in our intellectual cognition.

Regarding the third, the procedure is as follows. It seems that more universal things are not prior in our intellectual cognition: because those things which are prior and better known according to nature are posterior and less known according to us; but universals are prior according to the nature of our intellect. Furthermore, composites are prior to us compared to simple things, but universals are prior <unclear>cioza</unclear> <note>likely "simpliciora" or simpler</note>: therefore they are known later by us. Furthermore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the first book of the *Physics* that the defined thing first falls into our cognition, and the parts of the definition are less universal: just as "animal" is a part of the definition of "man": and universals are known later by us. Furthermore, we arrive at effects by chance and principles. But universals are known later by us. But if it is as stated in the first book of the *Physics*, one must descend from the books to singulars.

I respond that it must be said that in the cognition of our intellect, two things must be considered. First, indeed, that intellectual cognition in some way takes its beginning from sensitive cognition. And because the sense is of singulars and the intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the cognition of singulars, as far as we are concerned, be prior to the cognition of universals. Second, it must be considered that our intellect proceeds from potency to act. And that which proceeds from potency to act first reaches an incomplete act, which is the middle between potency and act, and then a perfect act. The perfect act to which the intellect arrives is complete science, through which things are known distinctly and determinately; the incomplete act is imperfect science, through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For what is known in this way is known both in act and in a certain way in potency. As is said in the first book of the *Physics*: things that are confused are first manifest and certain to us. Later, however, we know by distinguishing the principles and elements distinctly. It is manifest, moreover, that to know something in which many things are contained, without having proper knowledge of each of those things contained in it, is to know something under a certain confusion. In this way, both a whole in which parts are contained in potency and an integral whole can be known; for each whole can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being distinctly known. To know distinctly that which is contained in the whole is to have cognition of a less common thing: just as to know "animal" indistinctly is to know "animal" in which there is either the rational or the irrational, which is to know "man" or "lion." Therefore, it first occurs to our intellect to know "animal" before knowing "man." And the same reasoning holds if we compare anything more universal to the less universal, just as the sense goes from potency to act, so does the intellect: and this order

<column-break/>

of cognition appears in the sense. For more is distinguished by the sense more and when less is known in the distance through <unclear>opzebedit</unclear> <note>likely "percipitur" or perceived</note> to be a body, and then perceived to be an animal; and later it is perceived to be an animal and perceived to be a man, and first a man and then Socrates. Or it is pleasing and evident that a child from the beginning first distinguishes a man from a non-man; and children from the beginning call all men "fathers." Later, however, they determine each one, as is said in the first book of the *Physics*: things are manifest and that one knows something indistinctly still and in potency, or knows both the fiction and the principle, so also one knows the genus and is able to know the differences. And thus, in itself, indistinct cognition is the medium between potency and act. And that the cognition of singulars is prior as far as we are concerned, and universal cognition is sensitive cognition and intellectual cognition. If both the sense and the intellect have cognition, the greater is prior and the cognition of the lesser and common.

To the first, it must be said that it can be considered in two ways. In one way, that which is considered through the intention of truth. And since the intention of truth and the true are the same, it has a relationship to many things. It arrives at the abstraction of the intellect as an end in this way, while truly it is posterior. In the first book of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle's De Anima</note>, it is said that the universal is either nothing or it is posterior; but he also added more and placed universals as substances: and in this consideration it is true: more because particulars are not except through participation in the more universal subsisting things which are called Ideas. In another way, it can be considered in relation to the nature itself of "animality" or "humanity" as it is found in particulars. And thus there is a twofold order of nature. One according to the way of generation and time, since in that way those things which are imperfect and in potency are prior. And in this way the more universal is prior in nature, which appears manifestly in the generation of man and animal. For first an animal is generated, then a man: as is said in the book *On the Generation of Animals*. The other is the order of perfection or the intention of nature, just as act is simply prior in nature and that which is perfect is prior to that which is imperfect: and in this way the less universal is prior in nature, as "man" is prior to "animal." For the intention of nature does not stop at the generation of an animal, but intends to generate a man.

To the second, the more universal is compared to the less universal as a whole, and through the whole which is made, the more universal is not only common to man and horse: as it can be less and contains in the future not only the more universal but also others, as man is not only animal but rational. Thus, therefore, "animal" considered in itself is prior in our cognition to "man." If "man" is prior in our cognition to "animal," it is so through his reasoning.

To the third, it must be said that something can be known in two ways. In one way absolutely according to what it is in itself, and thus nothing is a house. In another way, since they are parts of this whole, like stones, it is necessary that we first know the whole and then the parts. For we first know the house in a certain confused way; thus it must be said that the defining parts, considered absolutely, are prior to us and the defined. Otherwise, the defined would not be made known through them. But they are more like parts.

<summary>Aquinas discusses the order of human knowledge, arguing that we naturally move from confused, universal concepts (like "animal") to distinct, specific ones (like "man"). He distinguishes between the order of nature, where the specific is prior as the goal, and the order of our learning, where the general precedes the particular.</summary>
<keywords>universals, cognition, intellect, potency and act, Aristotle, genus, species, generation, definition</keywords>

# Kalila and Dimna

<note>A small decorative floral-style border element appears at the top of the page.</note>

When the Lion woke the next morning, the Judge and a group of his prominent companions entered his presence with a written record of what Dimna had said in his <term>ma'adhir</term> <gloss>excuses or defenses</gloss>. The Lion took the document and ordered them to depart from him.

Then he sent for his mother and read the document to her. It distressed her, and she said: "If I am harsh with you, O King, do not be angry."

The Lion said: "I shall not be angry, so say what you wish."

She said: "I do not see you recognizing what harms you from what benefits you. I believe that as long as you continue to delay your decision regarding Dimna's case, he will stir up against you a trouble that you will be unable to withstand, whether sitting or standing."

Then she stood up and left in anger. When the next day came, the Judge sent for Dimna and brought him out. He consulted the <term>ulama</term> <gloss>scholars or learned men</gloss> regarding him, but they said nothing.

The Judge said to him: "Even if all those present are silent and say nothing, their suspicions have converged on the fact that you are a criminal. There is no good for you in life after the accusation has taken root in their hearts. I see nothing better for you than to confess your guilt, so that you may release your neck from the consequences of the afterlife. This would also restore a good reputation to your name for two reasons: first, your ability to find ways out and to fabricate <term>ma'adhir</term> <gloss>excuses</gloss> to defend yourself; and second, your confession of your sin, choosing safety in the afterlife over safety in this world. For the scholars have said: Death in what is honorable is better than life in what is <column-break/> shameful."

Dimna answered him, saying: "Judges do not rule based on their own suspicions, nor on the suspicions of the common people or the elite. I have known that suspicion is no substitute for the truth. Even if you all suspect that I am the perpetrator of this crime, I know myself best, and my knowledge of myself is a certainty in which there is no doubt. My situation has only become ugly in your eyes, if that is the case, because you suspect that I have acted maliciously."

A clamor arose throughout the entire city,
A disturbance in the imagination of that Sultan.
The hearts of the city's elite and commoners were lost,
Wondering what distress and calamity had occurred.
Is a conquering enemy intending to attack us?
Or has a celestial plague arisen from the Unseen?
For Dalqak has arrived in a rough, tattered cloak,
Having killed several swift horses along the road.
The people gathered at the King’s palace,
Asking why he arrived with such frantic haste.
From his speed, a foul exertion was evident;
A roar and agitation filled the city of Termez.
One person raised both hands in prayer,
While another, out of dread, cried out in woe.
From the outcry, the sedition, the fear, and the punishment,
Every heart was swept away by a hundred kinds of fancies.
Everyone made a prediction based on their own conjecture,
Wondering what fire had fallen into the wool.
The King quickly sought a path and gave him entry;
When he kissed the ground, the King said: "Hey, what happened?"
To anyone who asked of his condition in that bitterness,
He would place a finger to his lips, saying: "Hush!"
This behavior of his inflamed the King's imagination;
Everyone became stunned and paralyzed by the agitation.
Dalqak gestured: "O Munificent King,
Grant me a moment so that I may catch my breath,
Until my fleeting intellect returns to me,
For I have fallen into a wondrous world."
After an hour, during which the King’s throat and mouth
Grew bitter from the suspicion of his thoughts—
For he had never seen Dalqak in such a state,
As there was no companion more pleasant than him.
He used to always practice trickery and jesting;
He kept the King joyful and laughing.
He would make him laugh so much in his seat
That the King would clutch his belly, doubled over,
Until his body would break into a sweat from the force of laughter,
Falling forward from the intensity of his mirth.
Yet today, he is thus pale and bitter,
Placing a finger to his lips, saying: "O King, be silent!"
Imagination upon imagination, fancy upon fancy;
The King wondered what punishment would come upon him.
For the King’s heart was filled with grief and caution,
Because the Khwarazm-Shah was a great shedder of blood.
He had killed many kings of that region,
Either by guile or by the power of that stubborn one.
The King of Termez was trembling in his suspicion,
And Dalqak’s performance only increased that dread.
The King said: "Speak quickly, what is the situation?
From whom is this turmoil and agitation of yours?"
He replied: "I heard in the village that the King
Has issued a proclamation at every crossroads,
Saying: 'I want someone who, in three days,
Can reach Samarkand,' and if he is still successful,
'I have set aside treasures for him in exchange.'
When the purpose is achieved through the message,
I hurried to him for that reason,
To say that I do not have that ability!
Such a lowly task does not suit one like me;
Do not weave the thread of this hope upon me."

Your love, my poverty, youth, and the new spring;
