# The Nahid Maqama

Isa ibn Hisham narrated to us, saying:
I turned with a group of my companions to the courtyard of a tent seeking hospitality from its people. A man with a parched complexion came out to us and said: "Who are you?" We said: "Guests who have not tasted an enemy <note>idiom for food</note> for three days." He said: "Move aside." Then he said: "O youths, what do you think of a portion of <term>nahida</term> <gloss>a dish of butter and flour</gloss> as white as a bald man's pate, in a wide bowl, crowned with the froth of a great camel's hump, one portion of which fills the mouth? It is for a group of hungry, thirsty men on their fifth day without water. The tooth disappears into it, and its date-stones are like the tongues of birds. They gulp down the <term>nahida</term> with bowls of milk they have milked from old, sturdy camels. Do you desire it, O youths?" We said: "Yes, by God, we desire it!" The old man guffawed and said: "And your uncle <note>referring to himself</note> also desires it!"

Then he said: "What is your opinion, O youths, of fine white bread like pieces of silver ingots, arranged on a leather mat smelling of mimosa bark? A bright, clever, and nimble youth leaps to it, kneading it without shaking or rattling it. He makes it softer than a gentle king, then moistens it with milk or a heavy pestle. Then he turns to it, twists it, and leaves it in the corner of the oven until it rises without being overbaked. Then he goes to the wood of the <term>ghada</term> tree and lights the fire. When its flame dies down, he prepares its bed of hot ashes, then takes his dough and throws it in after perfecting its color. He spreads it out, covers it, and when it is cooked and ready, he heaps upon it hot stones until the two heats meet. When he covers them on the matching embers with a lid, and it splits open clearly, its crust resembling thin layers, and its redness like the red of the famous Hijazi dates known as 'Mother of Locusts' or 'Ibn Tab's cluster,' he pours over it white honey like snow until it sinks into the fats, and the heart of the bread drinks what is upon it. I present it to you and you swallow it in great gulps. Do you desire it, O youths?"

He said: Each of us craned our necks at his description, our mouths watered, and we smacked our lips. We said: "Yes, by God, we desire it!" parts out of one hundred and nine parts of a share. You set the share as one hundred and nine parts, then multiply thirteen by one hundred and nine parts and add eighty parts to that. It becomes one thousand four hundred and ninety-seven, and the husband's portion is three hundred and twenty-seven.

If a woman leaves two sisters and a husband, and bequeaths to a man the equivalent of a sister's portion minus one-eighth of what remains of the estate after the legacy, the calculation for this is to establish the <term>faridah</term> <gloss>legal distribution of inheritance</gloss> from twelve shares. Each sister receives one-third of what remains of the estate after the legacy. This is the estate minus the legacy. You know that one-eighth of what remains plus the legacy equals a sister's portion. One-eighth of what remains is one-eighth of the estate minus one-eighth of the legacy. Therefore, one-eighth of the estate minus one-eighth of the legacy plus the legacy equals a sister's portion. This is one-eighth of the estate and seven-eighths of the legacy. The entire estate equals three-eighths of the estate and three legacies and five-eighths of a legacy. Subtract three-eighths of the estate from the estate, and five-eighths of the estate remains, equaling three legacies and five-eighths of a legacy. The entire estate equals five legacies and four-fifths of a legacy. Thus, the estate is twenty-nine, the legacy is five, and the portion is eight.

In another type of legacy: a man dies and leaves four sons, and bequeaths to a man the equivalent of the portion of one of his sons, and to another man one-quarter of what remains of the third. Know that the legacy is only from the third.

<meta>continues from previous page: As for the error that occurs from someone other than this class of people, it is pure sin, whether the error is in theoretical or practical matters.</meta>

Therefore, just as an ignorant judge who is unfamiliar with the <term>Sunnah</term> <gloss>the traditions and practices of the Prophet</gloss> is not excused if he errs in a ruling, so too the one who judges concerning existing things is not excused if the conditions for judgment are not met in him. Rather, he is either a sinner or an infidel <note>original: "kafir"</note>. If it is required of a judge in matters of the permitted and the forbidden that the means of <term>ijtihad</term> <gloss>independent legal reasoning</gloss> be gathered in him—which is the knowledge of the <term>usul</term> <gloss>legal fundamentals</gloss> and the knowledge of <term>istinbat</term> <gloss>deduction</gloss> from those fundamentals by <term>qiyas</term> <gloss>analogy</gloss>—how much more so should this be required for the one who judges existing things? By this I mean that he must know the rational first principles and the method of deduction from them.

In short, error regarding the Law is of two kinds. First, there is an error for which a person is excused if they are among those qualified to investigate the matter in which the error occurred, just as a skilled physician is excused if he errs in the art of medicine, or a skilled judge is excused if he errs in a ruling; however, one who is not an expert in that field is not excused. Second, there is an error for which no one is excused. If such an error occurs regarding the principles of the Law, it is <term>kufr</term> <gloss>infidelity or unbelief</gloss>, and if it occurs in matters beyond the principles, it is <term>bid'ah</term> <gloss>unwarranted innovation</gloss>.

This second type of error concerns things that all classes of argumentative methods lead to knowing, such that knowledge of that thing is possible for everyone in this way. Examples of this include the acknowledgment of God, Blessed and Exalted is He, of the Prophethoods, and of the happiness and misery of the afterlife. This is because these three foundations are reached through the three types of evidence which <note>The author refers to the demonstrative, dialectical, and rhetorical methods of proof.</note>

<summary>Averroes argues that only qualified scholars are excused for errors in complex legal or philosophical interpretations. He defines fundamental tenets of faith that are accessible to all and thus mandatory to accept without error.</summary>

Its Sultan is King Badr al-Din ibn Qaraman <note>the name is pronounced with a short 'a' sound on the Qaf and the Ra</note>. Before him, it belonged to Ashqiya Musa, who surrendered it to King al-Nasir <note>the Mamluk Sultan of Egypt</note> in exchange for a compensation. Al-Nasir sent a governor and an army to the city, but later Sultan Badr al-Din seized control of it and built his royal residence there, establishing his rule. I met this Sultan outside the city as he was returning from a hunt. I dismounted from my beast for him, so he dismounted from his beast and greeted me. He welcomed me warmly. It is the custom of the kings of these lands that if a traveler dismounts for them, they are pleased by his action and increase their honor toward him; however, if he greets them while remaining mounted, they take offense and are displeased, which often leads to the traveler being deprived of their favor. This happened to me with one of them, and I regretted it. When I greeted him and remounted, he asked about my circumstances and my arrival. I entered the city with him, and he ordered that I be given the finest lodging. He used to send abundant food, fruit, and sweets in silver bowls, along with candles and robes of honor. He provided me with a mount and treated me excellently. Our stay with him was not long, and we departed for the city of Aqsaray <note>pronounced with a short 'a' on the Alif, a silent Qaf, and a short 'a' on the Sad and Ra</note>.

It is one of the most beautiful and well-constructed cities of the land of the <term>Rum</term> <gloss>Anatolia</gloss>. It is surrounded by flowing springs and orchards on every side. Three rivers flow through the city, and water runs through the houses. It contains many trees and grapevines, and there are many gardens within its walls. The famous carpets named after the city are manufactured there from sheep's wool; they have no equal in any other land. From there, they are exported to Syria, Egypt, Iraq, India, China, and the lands of the Turks. This city is under the authority of the King of Iraq <note>the Ilkhanid Mongol ruler</note>. I stayed there at the <term>zawiya</term> <gloss>hospice</gloss> of Sharif Husayn, the deputy there for Emir Arta. This Sharif is one of the <term>Fityan</term> <gloss>members of the youth brotherhoods</gloss> and has a large following. The Light of the world is for the natural or external man, and thus for those things which are in him. Although the things there do not appear to belong to that light, they nevertheless do; for nothing can be grasped by the natural man except through such things as exist and appear in the solar world, and thus unless they have some form from the light and shade there. All ideas of time and ideas of space, which are so important in the natural man that he cannot think without them, also belong to the light of the world. But the Light of heaven is for the spiritual or internal man. The interior mind of man, where his intellectual ideas—which are called immaterial—reside, is in that light. Man is unaware of this, even though he calls his understanding "sight" and ascribes "light" to it. The reason is that as long as he is in worldly and corporeal things, he only has a perception of such things as belong to the light of the world, but not of such things as belong to the light of heaven. The light of heaven is from the Lord alone; the entire heaven is in that light. This Light of heaven is immensely more perfect than the light of the world. Those things which make up a single ray in the light of the world make up myriads in the Light of heaven. Within the light of heaven there is intelligence and wisdom. That light is what flows into the light of the world which is in the External or Natural man, and enables him to perceive the objects of things through the senses. Unless that light flowed in, man would never have any perception, for those things which belong to the light of the world derive their life from it. # The Reason We Set the Distance

We have set the distance from the <term>nisf al-nahar</term> <gloss>midday/meridian</gloss> because the <term>ta'dil</term> <gloss>adjustment or equation</gloss> for the birth <note>referring to the calculation of the new moon or the birth of the month</note> is easier by it than by working with the horizons. The longest daylight hours for the latitude of Jerusalem are fourteen hours and a fraction. The Jewish practice of using <term>al-sa'at al-zamaniyya</term> <gloss>seasonal or temporal hours</gloss> is only correct if the <term>ijtima'</term> <gloss>conjunction</gloss> for the beginning of <term>Tishrei</term> <gloss>the first month of the Jewish civil year</gloss> occurs exactly at the autumnal equinox. However, it never occurs exactly with it; rather, it precedes or follows it by a significant amount, as we have explained previously.

When we extract the time of conjunction using the calculation provided by the Jews in the table which we have analyzed according to their opinion, we proceed from that to the knowledge of the first day of the year and the determination of its quality: whether it is <term>naqisan</term> <gloss>deficient</gloss>, <term>mu'tadilan</term> <gloss>regular</gloss>, or <term>tamman</term> <gloss>complete</gloss>. We already possess the knowledge of whether the year is <term>basita</term> <gloss>common/plain</gloss> or <term>kabisa</term> <gloss>leap/intercalary</gloss>. 

We then search in the Table of Limits for a duration of the days of the week whose two boundaries encompass the time we calculated for the conjunction. We look in the section for leap years if it is a leap year, and in the section for common years if it is a common year. When we find it, we find alongside it the first day of the year in the week and its quality. Once we know the start of the year and its quality, and combine that quality with its status as common or leap, we can determine from that the passing of the start of the following year.

Regarding the chapter titled "Complete Purification," it is called "Complete Purification" because it performs the act of purifying. That which causes all of existence to become free from faults is complete purification. In the chapter that clarifies this, it is also called the Chapter on Complete Purification. That which pervades all things is complete purification; it is <term>tathata</term> <gloss>suchness</gloss>, the emptiness of all phenomena. The word "expressed" refers to what was taught in the eighth chapter. The word "afterwards" refers to the present moment. The "deities" are the <term>Vajra-Gauri</term> and the others.

If one asks, "In what way is that which is impure purified?" the text says, "the six sense bases" and so forth. "By nature" means by the nature of suchness. If one asks, "If it is already pure, why must it be purified?" the text mentions "afflictions" and so forth. The obscuration of knowledge is the lack of understanding of the true nature; it is called the obscuration of ignorance. The afflictions are attachment and the rest; these are the obscurations of affliction. To be "obscured by them" means to be covered. For that reason, one performs complete purification. If one asks, "What is the nature of that purification which consists of suchness itself?" the text says, "the nature of self-awareness" and so forth.

The wind moves in and out through the two nostrils.

Until the first of the other movements.

Each day decreases by one stick.
The breaths, including the four quarters of the fierce one,

If one asks: "How is that which is the Great Bliss of the worldly ones the primary object of meditation?" It is said: "That which is called <term>Sahajananda</term> <gloss>Co-emergent Joy</gloss>," and so forth. 

Then, if one asks: "If you are the primary Great Bliss that is to be accomplished, and the co-emergent pleasure of <term>Samsara</term> <gloss>the cycle of existence</gloss> is not the object of accomplishment, why are you the primary object of accomplishment?" It is said: "If it is so, then I..." and so forth. The word "also" carries the meaning of "cause," because it establishes confidence in that very essence as the primary. Because the realization is established through a corresponding example, that very essence is designated as "I, the primary."

"Like a lamp in the darkness." This means that just as a lamp makes a pot or other objects in a dark room clearly understood, the Co-emergent Joy of the example makes the Great Bliss that is to be accomplished clear.

To clarify the meaning of the words "I dwell in <term>Sukhavati</term> <gloss>The Blissful Pure Land</gloss>," and so forth, it is said: "The teacher of the thirty..." and so forth. The "Consort" refers to the <term>Vajra</term> Consort <note>the wisdom consort in the context of the completion stage</note> and the consort of the example <note>the physical consort used in practice</note>. Consequently, those who seek the Great Bliss that is to be accomplished must certainly meditate on the <term>Devata Yoga</term> <gloss>Deity Yoga</gloss>. This is the intended meaning.

Regarding the statement "one does not truly perceive outer emptiness within inner emptiness," it means that inner emptiness is empty by its own essential nature. Thirdly, regarding the four bases of miraculous power <term>rddhipada</term> <gloss>literally "feet of miracles"</gloss>: they are called the bases of miraculous power because they serve as the foundation and the abiding place for the supramundane qualities known as miracles. These four are: aspiration, diligence, intention, and investigation.

In this regard, when some individuals generate a great desire to meditate on virtuous qualities, they apply themselves solely through the power of aspiration. Without any other distinct thoughts or mental engagements, the mind becomes one-pointed. The meditative concentration <term>samadhi</term> produced through the power of that aspiration is called the "meditative concentration of aspiration."

Some, when applying themselves through the diligence of the four correct abandonments, apply themselves with the diligence that establishes virtue. When they enter into the process of abandoning non-virtue and generating virtue, the mind becomes one-pointed. The meditative concentration produced through the power of that diligence is called the "meditative concentration of diligence."

Some, when entering into the training of the mind, perfectly place the mind through the causes of calm abiding <term>shamatha</term>, holding the mind, and equanimity. # The Explanation of the Noble Four Dharmas

Homage to Manjushri, the youthful.

Why was this <term>sutra</term> <gloss>scriptural discourse</gloss> composed, which states: "A <term>bodhisattva mahasattva</term> <gloss>great heroic being of awakening</gloss> should not abandon these four <term>dharmas</term> <gloss>qualities or teachings</gloss> for as long as they live, even for the sake of their life"?

It was composed to correctly show the methods for attaining unsurpassed awakening to those who are confused about entering the Great Vehicle <note>Mahayana</note>. It is to cause the heedless to correctly adopt the practice, to uplift those who are discouraged, and to bring joy to those who have correctly entered the path.

The number "four" is mentioned to prevent the rejection of the teachings by those who might fear they are too extensive. By stating the number, they are easily remembered. Furthermore, the qualities of patience and gentleness, which appear below, are not differentiated because they serve a single purpose.

Although there are many categories of those who have correctly entered the Great Vehicle, two names <note>Bodhisattva and Mahasattva</note> are mentioned for three reasons: interest, application, and realization.

How is it by interest? One is a <term>bodhisattva</term> <gloss>awakening being</gloss> because of interest in the profound objects of knowledge. One is a <term>mahasattva</term> <gloss>great being</gloss> because of interest in great power.

How is it by application? It is because one strives for the sake of one's own unsurpassed, perfect awakening, and for the sake of fully protecting all sentient beings from suffering.

How is it by realization? It is because awakening is realized through two strengths. What are the two? The strength of intelligence and the strength of diligence. One cannot realize awakening through ignorance or through small diligence.

### ON ALCHEMY

<margin>The end of Alchemy is not gold and silver, but secrets.</margin>
<margin>Poison even in the best things.</margin>
Who is there who would dare to deny that poison lies hidden and exists even in the best things? Everyone is compelled to confess this. If this is true, I now ask you whether the poison should not be separated from the good and useful? And the good accepted, the evil left behind? Indeed, it must be so. If, therefore, it is necessary, I pray you, tell me how it is separated in your workshops? For among you, everything remains mixed together. But so that you may protect your simplicity, if you are convicted into confessing that poison lies hidden there and are asked where it finally goes, then you bring forth I know not what concerning "corrections" which are supposed to drive out and take away the poison, <margin>The correction of Physicians is examined.</margin> just as they say Quince corrects <term>Scammony</term> <gloss>a harsh purgative resin</gloss>, and later <term>Diagridium</term> <gloss>purified scammony</gloss>. But what kind of correction is that? Does the poison not remain afterward just as it was at first? And yet you meanwhile boast that you have corrected it, so much so that the poison no longer harms. But where did it escape to? <margin>Diagridion.</margin> It remains in the Diagridium. Try it, if you are wise: exceed the limit, and you will see where the poison is. For you will know it quite quickly. Thus you also correct <term>Turbith</term> <gloss>an Ayurvedic purgative root</gloss>, and you call it <term>Diaturbith</term>. Such are your corrections, which would be fit for peasants and should be given to pack-horses. Make the danger by exceeding the limit and increase the dose: you will see if you do not feel the poison. <margin>What it is to correct a Medicine.</margin> *To correct is to take what has been corrected.* He who is malicious and has sinned: if he is punished, the correction does not extend further than the will of him who was punished lasts. Such are these corrections also; the power lies with the substances themselves, not with you. Now, in this case, a Physician must consider nothing further than that the poison be removed. This must be done through separation. As, for example: a serpent is poisonous, and yet it is adopted for food. If you remove the poison from it, you may eat it with no harm. The same must be understood equally concerning all other things, namely that there is need for a similar separation. Until that is done, you cannot be secure in your operation, unless by chance it happens that nature supplies your deficiencies, or a greater benevolence of the heavens favors you. For in your art, no protection will have remained.

Now, therefore, at last, if that true foundation which takes away poison is required, let us see how Alchemy provides it. For it is necessary that it be done in such a way that, if Mars is in the Sun, Mars is removed; and if Saturn is in Venus, he is separated from her. For as many ascendants and impressions as there are in the things of nature, so many bodies also exist in them. But as for those bodies which are contrary, it is altogether necessary that some of them be removed and taken away, so that in this way all contrariety is abolished, and the evil is removed from the good which you seek. <margin>Fire perfects all things.</margin> Just as gold is useful for nothing unless it is first cast into the fire, so a Medicine is much less useful which does not pass through the fire. For it is necessary for all things to pass through the fire into a second generation, by which it ought to benefit and help man. And should this not deservedly be judged the upright foundation of any Physician? For a Physician ought not to apply poisons, but rather <term>arcana</term> <gloss>secret virtues</gloss>. <margin>The workshops are rebuked.</margin> However, all those workshop preparations, as many as there are, do not contribute even a single letter to this doctrine; but they are occupied simply in "correcting," as if a dog farted in a room, and that stench were lulled either by lozenges and incense, or by juniper wood: I ask you, does the stench not remain in the room afterward just as before? And although it may not be perceived by the sense of smell, is it therefore lawful for anyone to say the stench has been separated and no longer remains? Indeed, it is present, but corrected by the fumigation. Thus, therefore, the fumigation and the foul air enter the nostrils together. Of this kind also are the corrections of the Pharmacists, who blunt an <term>Aleopaticum</term> <note>likely a reference to a bitter or purging medicine</note> with sugar, so that it may inflict no harm. But if the power of a greater natural heat should reach that quicksilver before it is formed into its final state—namely, into the shape of silver—so that it is reduced into the pure and red sulfur of Nature, then gold is made from it more quickly than silver. It remains in that state perpetually once the end toward which Nature tends by its labor is achieved.

Quicksilver, which we have just mentioned, is the mother of all metals because of its coldness and moisture. If it is made pure and separated from all superfluity, then no further thickness can be mixed with it, so that it might be reduced back into some imperfect metal. For Nature does not work backward, nor is it a matter that looks toward any impure form, such as the imperfect metals are. But sulfur is the father of all metals because of its heat and dryness. According to this difference, let it be observed that quicksilver is described in the following chapter.

## CHAPTER II.

There is, therefore, in all metals a true Mercury and a right sulfur, equally in the imperfect as in the perfect metals. It has merely been contaminated and made impure in the imperfect metals, which alone are destitute of perfect maturation. For these same reasons, they can be reduced to gold and silver; that is, so that the impurity with which they were defiled may be separated from the golden or silver nature that is within them, and the form of gold or silver may be introduced into them. For they were torn away from Nature because they were removed and dug out from their natural passages, mines, and veins of the earth. Therefore, they can no longer have any operation within themselves as if they were still hiding under the earth; nevertheless, as much as is in them, they desire to be perfected.
